newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Modelo exports set pace in Q1.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Modelo exports set pace in Q1.

text.p: Top Mexican brewer Grupo Modelo SA de CV bounced back from a lackluster fourth quarter to post better-than-expected results for the first three months of 1997, analysts said on Tuesday.

In short, Modelo's exports boomed, exceeding even the company's best forecasts for the first quarter by growing 23.1 percent compared with the first quarter of 1996, while operating income jumped 13.7 percent.

"The results all around were higher that what we expected, above all in the margin," said Alonso Madero, a beverage analyst with BBV-Probursa in Mexico City, referring a first-quarter operating margin of 20.2 percent compared with 17.3 percent in the year-earlier period.

Modelo posted earnings of 0.33 pesos, a little better than the average 0.32 pesos forecast by three analysts surveyed by Reuters. But operating income came in much higher than forecast at 609.40 million pesos. Analysts had expected operating income of 432 million pesos.
Gross profit (1.494 billion pesos vs. 1.310 billion pesos) and revenues (3.021 billion pesos vs. 2.959 billion pesos) also exceeded forecasts.
The surprise in export growth came not in Modelo's showcase Corona brand (up 20 percent), but rather with Pacifico (up 94 percent), Modelo Especial (up 60 percent) and Negra Modelo (up 26 percent).
"Remember when Corona was the real 'in' brand with the young crowd. Now I think that new young crowd is starting to go for Pacifico," said Scott Weiss, an analyst with D.A. Campbell in Los Angeles.
Corona remains Modelo's top export brand, and it is second only to Heineken among all imported beer in the United States. About 80 percent of Modelo's exports go to the U.S. market.

"We have a target of export growth between 15 and 20 percent for the year and this puts us on track," said Emilio Fulloando, Modelo's director of investor relations. "The U.S. market normally is slow in the first quarter because of the winter months, but it responded very well to our products."
The strong operating results reflected several factors, including a 23 percent price increase in March and lower grain and packaging costs.
Modelo said in its press release that the cost of goods sold fell by 6.1 percent because of "efficiencies obtained in the production process."

A big question for analysts was how much of the depreciation costs for the new Modelo plant in Zacatecas state the company would charge to the first quarter and how much it would defer to the second quarter. The plant came on line March 14.
Fulloando could not provide an exact figure. "We're still looking at this, and next month we expect to have more information," he said.
Domestic sales volume were flat, as expected, even with the March price increase. Analysts viewed that as a positive sign for the Mexican beer market for the rest of the year.

"It shows that there is a lot of stability in pricing and volumes," said Carlos Laboy, a beverage analyst with Bear Stearns in New York. "The orderliness of the Mexican beer market is what stands out most."
Domestically, Modelo's first-quarter sales volume dipped to 5.719 million hectoliters from 5.731 million hectoliters in the first quarter of last year.
Overall, Modelo sold 6.735 million hectoliters in Mexico and abroad in the first quarter, just below the 6.78 million forecast in the Reuters survey.
